title: The State of Public Education in 2026 in Five Charts
gist: RAND's 2026 survey data show U.S. public education under sustained strain: teacher burnout and low retention intent persist despite modest year-over-year improvement, students keep adopting AI for homework even as most believe it erodes critical thinking, chronic absenteeism has fallen but stays well above pre-pandemic levels, stricter phone bans reduce but don't eliminate in-class phone checking, and pre-K teachers lack curriculum materials adequate for diverse learners.

insights.claim: In RAND's 2026 State of the American Teacher survey, only one in four U.S. public-school teachers said they planned to stay in the profession as long as they were able, indicating a large share are looking toward an early exit.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Points to continued elevated teacher attrition risk, which sustains demand for substitute-teacher staffing, tutoring/remediation services, and teacher-recruitment/retention edtech even as raw stress metrics improve.
insights.quote: In 2026, only one in four said they planned to stay in the profession as long as they were able.
insights.locator: Teachers Are Still Burning Out, and Managing Student Behavior Is a Top Source of Their Stress

insights.claim: Teacher-reported frequent job-related stress fell to 55% in 2026 from a 2021 high of 78%, but still runs roughly 20 percentage points above the 34% rate reported by similar working adults, showing the gap has narrowed only modestly since the pandemic peak.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: The persistent teacher/general-workforce well-being gap is a structural, multi-year condition rather than a pandemic-era blip, implying the teacher-shortage/retention problem is durable and not self-correcting quickly.
insights.locator: Figure 1. Well-Being of Teachers and Similar Working Adults

insights.claim: The top driver of teacher job stress is managing student behavior, followed by low pay and excessive working hours, which RAND links directly to chronic student absenteeism and poor student mental health as underlying causes.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Behavior-management burden, not just compensation, is the primary stressor — suggesting interventions aimed only at pay (e.g., raises) may under-deliver on retention unless paired with student-behavior and mental-health supports.
insights.locator: The top source of job-related stress is managing student behavior

insights.claim: The author frames persistently poor teacher well-being as a risk not just to individual educators but to instructional continuity, since student outcomes depend on having stable, experienced teachers in the classroom.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Ties teacher well-being metrics directly to a downstream human-capital/learning-outcomes risk, relevant to any long-horizon assessment of U.S. public education quality and workforce readiness.
insights.quote: Persistently poor teacher well-being matters not only for educators themselves but also for the students who depend on having a stable, experienced teacher.
insights.locator: Teachers Are Still Burning Out, and Managing Student Behavior Is a Top Source of Their Stress

insights.claim: 67% of youth surveyed in December 2025 agreed or strongly agreed that increased student use of AI tools like ChatGPT for schoolwork harms critical thinking skills, even as AI use for homework has continued to rise over the prior 18 months.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: A majority-skeptical user base that keeps adopting the product anyway is a classic convenience-over-trust pattern; AI-in-education vendors face a persistent reputational/regulatory overhang even as usage and revenue potential grow.
insights.quote: Sixty-seven percent of youth surveyed in December 2025 agreed or strongly agreed that the more students use AI for their schoolwork, the more it will harm their critical thinking skills.
insights.locator: Two-Thirds of Students Agree That Using AI More for Schoolwork Harms Their Critical Thinking

insights.claim: Skepticism about AI's harm to critical thinking rises with age/grade level: 36% of college students strongly agreed it's harmful versus 18% of middle schoolers, while the students who use AI for three or more classes were less likely to strongly agree (22%) than those not using AI at all (35%).
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Heavier AI users report comparatively less alarm about it than non-users, suggesting either habituation/normalization among users or self-selection — a nuance that matters for interpreting survey-based backlash narratives against AI-in-education tools.
insights.locator: Figure 2. Percentage of Students Who Agreed or Strongly Agreed That Using AI More for Schoolwork Will Harm Critical Thinking Skills, by Grade

insights.claim: The students most skeptical of AI's effect on critical thinking are precisely those who are not currently using it for homework help, an inverse relationship between usage and stated concern that the author explicitly flags as notable.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Undercuts a simple narrative that AI use itself drives concern about cognitive harm; investors evaluating edtech-AI adoption curves should treat stated-skepticism survey data as only weakly predictive of actual usage decline.
insights.quote: The sharpest skeptics, however, are students who are not currently using AI for help with their homework.
insights.locator: Two-Thirds of Students Agree That Using AI More for Schoolwork Harms Their Critical Thinking

themes.theme: Chronic Absenteeism: Improving but Structurally Elevated

insights.claim: Nationwide chronic absenteeism (missing 10%+ of school days) rose from a pre-pandemic baseline of about 15% (2017-2020) to a peak of 29% in 2021-2022, and RAND's own survey-based estimate shows it declining to 18% in the 2025-2026 school year — still roughly three percentage points above the pre-pandemic norm five years after schools reopened.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Absenteeism is normalizing but not fully reverting, implying a persistent drag on average daily attendance-linked school funding formulas and on measured academic recovery timelines in many U.S. states.
insights.locator: Figure 3. Chronic Absenteeism Rates by School Year and Percentage of Students Who Were Absent

insights.claim: Higher chronic absenteeism rates predict lower academic achievement and higher dropout risk, and urban school districts currently show the highest absenteeism rates among U.S. public schools.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Urban districts carrying the highest absenteeism concentrate the achievement/dropout risk geographically, a relevant filter for any muni-bond, school-funding, or urban-education-policy analysis.
insights.quote: Higher rates predict lower academic achievement and higher dropout risk, meaning every school year in which rates remain elevated represents a real cost to students' futures.
insights.locator: Chronic Absenteeism Is Falling—but Remains Well Above Pre-Pandemic Levels

insights.claim: RAND explicitly cautions that it is not clear pre-pandemic attendance norms will fully reset on their own, treating the current decline as reason for only cautious optimism rather than a resolved problem.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Signals continued multi-year uncertainty in attendance normalization — a slow-moving, monitorable trend rather than a near-term resolved issue.
insights.quote: It's not clear that attendance norms will fully reset on their own.
insights.locator: Chronic Absenteeism Is Falling—but Remains Well Above Pre-Pandemic Levels

themes.theme: Smartphone Restriction Policies: Effective but Not a Full Fix

insights.claim: Among five distinct types of school cell-phone policies RAND identified, students in schools that ban bringing phones entirely checked their phones at least once per class only 42% of the time, versus 84% in schools where phone use in class is left to teacher discretion — showing a clear gradient where stricter policies correlate with less in-class phone checking.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Validates that policy strictness meaningfully changes behavior, relevant to districts and vendors of phone-restriction enforcement tools (lockable pouches, phone lockers) deciding how strict a policy to implement or sell against.
insights.locator: Figure 4: Percentage of Students Who Checked Their Cell Phones During Their Classes at Least Once per Day, by School Cell Phone Policy

insights.claim: Even under the strictest policy studied — students cannot bring a phone to school at all — 42% of students still reported checking their phone at least once per class daily, meaning the most restrictive approach mitigates but does not eliminate in-class phone use.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic ceiling on what phone-ban policy alone can achieve, implying diminishing returns on ever-stricter enforcement and possible residual demand for complementary interventions (education, alternative devices, monitoring).
insights.quote: policies that are more restrictive about where and when students can use their phones are associated with reduced percentages of students checking their devices.
insights.locator: Students and Smartphones: More-Restrictive Policies Seem to Mitigate—Not Eliminate—the Problem

insights.claim: The spread of student cell-phone restriction policies across U.S. public schools has been driven by rising concerns over smartphone overreliance and evidence linking phone use to poor student mental health and distracted learning.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Confirms mental-health and distraction concerns (not just academic performance) as the policy driver, a durable rationale that supports continued district-level adoption of phone-restriction measures nationally.
insights.locator: Students and Smartphones: More-Restrictive Policies Seem to Mitigate—Not Eliminate—the Problem

themes.theme: Pre-K Curriculum Gap for Diverse Learners

insights.claim: 85% of public pre-K teachers reported using multiple instructional materials rather than relying on a single comprehensive curriculum, typically combining a comprehensive material with several other resources to cover their classroom's needs.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: High mixing-and-matching rates signal that no single commercial pre-K curriculum product currently satisfies classroom needs, pointing to a fragmented market opportunity for a more comprehensive, differentiation-capable curriculum offering.
insights.quote: Eighty-five percent of pre-K teachers reported using multiple instructional materials, often combining comprehensive curriculum materials with many other resources.
insights.locator: Pre-K Teachers Lack Adequate Materials to Support Children's Diverse Learning Needs

insights.claim: Only about half of pre-K teachers said their instructional materials were adequate for supporting children with diverse learning needs, such as children with disabilities or English learners.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: A near-50% inadequacy rate in a foundational-skills-critical age band is a measurable, sizable unmet-need gap for curriculum publishers targeting special education and English-learner differentiation in early childhood education.
insights.quote: Only about half of pre-K teachers said their materials were adequate for supporting children with diverse learning needs, such as children with disabilities or English learners.
insights.locator: Pre-K Teachers Lack Adequate Materials to Support Children's Diverse Learning Needs

insights.claim: When providing additional support to struggling students or those with IEPs/IFSPs, pre-K teachers rely far more heavily on self-created materials (56-57%) and the Teachers Pay Teachers marketplace (36-44%) than on their comprehensive curriculum materials (28-33%), even though comprehensive materials are used by nearly all teachers (98%) for whole-class instruction.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Shows commercial curriculum materials are trusted for baseline instruction but not for differentiated/special-needs support, leaving an unregulated marketplace (TPT) and ad hoc teacher-made content to fill a quality-control gap — a risk for consistency of outcomes and an opening for curriculum vendors who can build in differentiation.
insights.locator: Figure 5: Percentage of Teachers Who Reported Using Each Type of Material for Groups of Students

insights.claim: The author frames early childhood (when foundational language, literacy, and numeracy skills take root) as precisely the wrong developmental window to leave teachers without adequate materials to serve every child.
insights.speaker: Julia H. Kaufman
insights.so_what: Frames the pre-K materials gap as a high-leverage, time-sensitive policy and market problem rather than a minor operational inconvenience, useful context for prioritizing early-childhood edtech/curriculum investment over later-grade interventions.
insights.quote: The earliest years of education, when foundational skills in language, literacy, and numeracy take root, is precisely the wrong time to leave teachers without the tools they need to support every child.
insights.locator: Pre-K Teachers Lack Adequate Materials to Support Children's Diverse Learning Needs
